cue: Hold the phone level. The sky above is pressed into the top of the picture, as a duck keeps it in view with its head down.

cpd.note: the median bird, standing in for an unmeasured duck

sat.note: a slight lift for the fourth cone

fold.note: how much of what lies above the horizon is pressed into the top

horizon.note: where the fold begins, in screen heights from the middle

blindAt.note: the blind area's direction, behind the head

blindDeg.note: the blind area's width; narrow in geese, none in dabbling ducks

band.note: the ribbon's height in screen heights

fadeS.note: seconds a direction stays in the ribbon

field.name: fold
field.note: the sky above the horizon pressed into the top of the picture (the draft's new effect)

field.name: ribbon
field.note: a band along the bottom keeps every direction the phone has faced, fading with age, so the whole circle a duck sees fills in as you turn

field.name: wedge
field.note: a goose's narrow blind area behind the head, fixed in the room as you turn the phone

field.name: squeeze
field.note: the view without the field options

rows: A mallard sees all the way around itself and over its head. Its two eyes overlap in a narrow strip, about 22 degrees wide, that runs from the bill up over the crown to the back of the head.
A dabbling duck cannot see below the level of its bill. Ducks that feed by filtering water find their food by touch instead, with sensitive tips on their bills.

Grazing geese and swans can see their bill tip and keep a blind area behind the head, where dabbling ducks see all around. With &draw=wedge and the motion sensors on, the blind area stays behind where you started as you turn.

Ducks have four kinds of colour-sensing cells, one more than people, and the fourth responds to violet light. A mallard's eye blocks most ultraviolet light before it reaches those cells, so this view adds no ultraviolet tint.
This part of the view is a guess. It assumes that a duck sees about a fifth as much detail as a person, the middle value for birds.
This part of the view is a guess. It assumes that a duck sees flicker about as fast as a pigeon or a chicken and runs the picture slightly slow.
The fold that presses the sky into the top of the picture, the ribbon of every direction faced, the blind area's width and the colour lift are the app's drawings.
Many ducks find food by feel, with the many touch-sensing cells at the tip of the bill. This view cannot show touch.
